blocks.text: 1. L1 Regularization

blocks.alt: The loss function gets an added L1 penalty, forming L1 regularization

blocks.text: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff, the previous topic's closing strategy, described deliberately trading a small amount of increased bias for a genuinely larger reduction in variance. L1 Regularization is the first genuinely concrete technique that actually applies that strategy in practice.

It works by adding a penalty directly to the loss function, based on the weights themselves, a genuinely direct, mathematical way of discouraging a network from relying too heavily on any single weight becoming genuinely too large.
2. The Core Idea

This connects back to any loss function already covered in the Loss Functions module. L1 Regularization adds a new term to that existing loss: the sum of the absolute values of every single weight in the network.

Larger weights now contribute a genuinely larger penalty to the total loss, meaning the network is directly, mathematically discouraged from letting any individual weight grow unnecessarily large during training.

blocks.text: 3. Why Penalize Weights At All

This connects back to overfitting, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Genuinely large weights often signal a model relying too heavily on a few specific features, exactly the kind of memorization-prone behavior already covered as overfitting in its own topic.

Discouraging large weights directly, through the penalty already covered in the previous section, pushes a network toward relying more evenly across its inputs, a genuinely more robust, generalizable pattern than depending heavily on just a few, specific weights.
4. The Sparsity Property

blocks.alt: The L1 penalty pushes some weights to reach exactly zero

blocks.text: A genuinely distinctive, important property of L1 specifically is that its penalty can push some weights all the way to exactly zero, not merely smaller, but genuinely, completely zero.

This effectively removes that specific input's influence from the model entirely, a genuinely unique behavior that sets L1 Regularization apart from other regularization approaches covered later in this module.
5. An Automatic Feature Selection Effect

blocks.alt: A zero weight means the feature is effectively removed

blocks.text: This connects back to Feature Selection, already covered in genuine depth in the traditional Machine Learning course. L1 Regularization performs a genuinely similar function automatically, during training itself, rather than as a genuinely separate, preliminary step.

Weights driven to exactly zero, already covered in the previous section, effectively identify which inputs the model actually considers genuinely important, a direct, built-in byproduct of training with L1 Regularization rather than a separately applied technique.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This automatic feature selection effect is genuinely valuable beyond just improving generalization. It can also reveal which input features a trained model actually considers meaningful, a useful insight in its own right.

blocks.text: 6. The Regularization Strength

A genuinely important hyperparameter, commonly called lambda, controls the regularization strength. A larger lambda produces a stronger penalty, pushing more weights toward exactly zero, already covered in the previous sections.

A smaller lambda produces a weaker penalty instead, keeping training closer to plain, unregularized behavior, a genuine, tunable knob covered further in the Hyperparameter Tuning module later in this course.
7. Connecting Back to Bias-Variance

blocks.alt: L1 regularization brings more bias but less variance

blocks.text: This connects back to the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, already covered in its own dedicated topic. L1 Regularization deliberately increases bias slightly, since it constrains the model away from perfectly fitting the training data.

This happens in direct exchange for a genuinely larger reduction in variance, exactly the deliberate tradeoff already covered as this module's own unifying strategy, now applied through this topic's specific, concrete technique.
8. A Genuine Computational Consideration

A genuine, real practical detail is that the absolute value function has a sharp corner at exactly zero, not smoothly differentiable there, a genuinely different mathematical behavior than L2 Regularization, covered in the very next topic.

This sharp corner is actually directly connected to the sparsity property already covered earlier in this topic, since this exact mathematical shape is what allows L1's penalty to genuinely push weights all the way to zero, rather than merely toward it.
9. Recognizing When L1 Regularization Is Genuinely Right

blocks.alt: Wanting a sparse model points toward using L1 regularization

blocks.text: Suspecting many input features are genuinely irrelevant is a direct case for L1 Regularization, its automatic, built-in feature selection, already covered throughout this topic, directly helping identify and remove those irrelevant inputs.

Wanting a genuinely simpler, more interpretable final model is another genuine case, since sparse, mostly-zero weights are considerably easier to actually interpret than a model where every single input contributes some small, non-zero amount.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates L1 Regularization's sparsity property, training a model with many irrelevant features and observing which weights actually get driven to zero.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso  # Lasso is scikit-learn's name for L1-regularized linear regression

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
n_samples, n_features = 200, 20
X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features))

# Only the first 3 features are actually genuinely relevant; the other 17 are pure noise
true_weights = np.zeros(n_features)
true_weights[:3] = [3.0, -2.0, 1.5]
y = X @ true_weights + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n_samples)

model = Lasso(alpha=0.1)  # alpha here is the lambda regularization strength covered in this topic
model.fit(X, y)

print("Learned weights (first 3 are genuinely relevant, the rest are pure noise):")
for i, weight in enumerate(model.coef_):
    marker = " <- genuinely relevant" if i < 3 else ""
    print(f"  Feature {i}: {weight:.4f}{marker}")

zero_count = np.sum(np.abs(model.coef_) < 1e-6)
print(f"\nNumber of weights driven to exactly zero: {zero_count} out of {n_features}")
print("L1 Regularization correctly identified which features are genuinely relevant, exactly the sparsity property covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example typically shows L1 Regularization correctly driving most, or all, of the 17 genuinely irrelevant features' weights to exactly zero, while keeping the 3 genuinely relevant features' weights meaningfully non-zero.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: L1 Regularization adds a penalty to the loss based on the sum of absolute weight values.
Larger weights contribute a genuinely larger penalty, directly discouraging any single weight from growing too large.
It can push some weights all the way to exactly zero, a genuinely distinctive property called sparsity.
This performs automatic feature selection during training, identifying which inputs the model considers relevant.
Lambda, the regularization strength, controls how aggressively weights get pushed toward zero.
It deliberately trades a small amount of increased bias for a genuinely larger reduction in variance.
The absolute value function's sharp corner at zero is directly connected to its sparsity-inducing behavior.
It genuinely fits situations with many suspected irrelevant features, or a need for a simpler, interpretable model.
Next up: L2 Regularization, a closely related technique with a genuinely different mathematical shape and behavior.
